summary: The note is a news-style feature on the rapid rise of the Virtual Party, an online-born political movement that won legislative seats worldwide by November 2, 2024. It covers the party's founding by Sara J. McKinsey, its direct-democracy platform, technology-driven campaigning, global spread, and policy proposals. It also records skepticism from traditional politicians and the debate over digital representation.
one_line: A news feature on the Virtual Party, an online-born movement founded by Sara J. McKinsey that won legislative seats worldwide by late 2024.
key_facts: The Virtual Party began as an online platform for policy debate and had clinched significant legislative seats around the world by November 2, 2024.
Sara J. McKinsey, a former technology entrepreneur, introduced the Virtual Party on September 3, 2023, through a manifesto video that went viral overnight.
McKinsey called for a "democratic reboot" leveraging the internet's democratizing potential.
Members of the Virtual Party debate, vote on policies, and select candidates through a secure online platform.
The party uses cryptocurrencies for funding, blockchain for ballot integrity, and AI algorithms to tailor political messaging.
By October 2024 the party had a following of millions, reaching nations such as Germany, India, and Canada, with early appeal in Seoul and São Paulo.
Several Virtual Party candidates won key races in the U.S. midterm elections, challenging the two-party system.
Jade Thompson, a 26-year-old virtual reality developer, became the first Virtual Party candidate to win a seat in the UK House of Commons after a campaign run entirely online.
The party uses YouTube for policy announcements, Twitch for live Q&A sessions, TikTok for satire and Gen-Z engagement, and virtual town halls.
Senator Robert Clarkson, 60, who has served in the U.S. Congress for three decades, said, "We need more than digital parlor tricks to govern a nation."
Policy proposals include a restructured tax system targeting wealth accumulated by tech giants, a rigorous data protection framework, and a carbon-neutral infrastructure blueprint.
The party's education initiative, "Code for All," promotes digital literacy programs to bridge the digital divide.

Critics say digital interaction may undermine democratic representation, while proponents compare it to postal voting, electronic voting machines, and television debates, once controversial but now accepted.
